emb_line: 129 test items have a training prompt at cosine 0.95 or more; the n-gram rules had already flagged 97 of those pairs. Of the 32 they missed, 8 are the same question: four MMLU maths items shorter than eight tokens ("Evaluate $\log_8 2$."), which no 8- or 13-gram rule can match at all, and questions reworded or reformatted; 21 are variants with other numbers. In a labelled sample of 27 pairs between 0.88 and 0.95: 1 reworded copy (a GSM8K test problem whose training-split twin tells the same story in other words), 9 variants, 17 merely similar. That is Tulu 3's complaint in numbers: below about 0.95 the score does not separate a paraphrase from a cousin, and a judge has to read the pair.
pr1_answer: About 170: 173 of 5,000 rows (3.5%), 54 of them because of the single n-gram of twelve zeros, the rest on maths notation n-grams such as "frac 0 0 frac 0 0". By reading, none of the Tulu 3 SFT rows here contains a test question (2 rows share a 13-gram or pass Tulu's rule, all stock phrases). The same filter run against the SFT rows with numbers kept would remove almost nothing.
pr3_answer: None. 43 web documents share a 13-gram with some test item; reading every flagged pair, 75 pairs are famous passages the items quote (speeches, novels, statutes), 54 are stock phrases and question stems, 1 is the WikiHow source of a HellaSwag item, and 0 contain a test question. (In the two whole FineWeb files read afterwards, four pages out of 1.45 million do; section 3.)
rlvr_line: Tulu 3's RLVR set (all 29,946 prompts, whose MATH part is the MATH training split with four worked examples in front of each question) contains 70 MMLU test questions word for word, every one from high-school mathematics (70 of its 270 items, 26%); for 65 of them the RLVR reward key equals MMLU's correct answer. MMLU's high-school maths items evidently include problems that are also in MATH's training split (the MMLU paper says its questions were collected from online sources; it does not name MATH). Measured over all of MMLU this is 0.50% of items, far below Tulu 3's 2% dataset threshold, which is why a benchmark-level rule cannot see it. UltraFeedback's 5,000 rows include one prompt that uses 2 ARC-Easy test questions, with options and answers, as few-shot examples.
dt_line: Its default indexes only n-grams of the answer and n-grams that straddle the end of the question and the start of the answer. In an MMLU item the question ends with the four options, which a RLVR row does not contain, so the default removed 434 RLVR rows and caught 1 of the 71 rows labelled copy. Switching on question n-grams (find_query_ngrams=True) catches 69 of 71, and removes 877 rows (2.9%), most of them on instruction phrases and number patterns. Which n-grams you index decides what you catch.
variant_line: 35 MATH-500 test problems have a sibling in RLVR's MATH training problems: the same diagram or opening with another question or other numbers (the altitudes of a triangle with angles 54 and 52 degrees in the test, 46 and 71 in training). One of these was first labelled a copy by the rules: z^4 + z^2 + 1 in the test, z^4 - z^2 + 1 in training, identical after punctuation is stripped. Variants teach the method, not the answer; GSM1k-style perturbed test sets exist to measure exactly that gap. GSM8K: 3 test items share an opening with a GSM8K training problem in RLVR, all variants.
fp_line: In RLVR alone 97 flagged pairs are answer-format instructions ("where m and n are relatively prime positive integers. Find m+n", "Enter the letter of the correct option") and 59 are shared Asymptote code (17 MATH-500 items, one preamble of 250 tokens reused by many graph problems); 27 MATH-500 items are matched by such phrases. GPT-3's remedy, ignoring n-grams that match more than 10 training documents, would remove most of these and keep the copies, which match one or two rows each.
web_line: The web samples share 13-grams with 62 (item, corpus) combinations, nearly all MMLU history and US-history items that quote a famous text: Kennedy's moon speech, Roosevelt's Pearl Harbor address, Dr King's letter from Birmingham, Patrick Henry, Dickens, the Declaration of Independence. Pages quote the speech, never the question. Nemotron-CC's synthetic question-answer rewrites add stock stems ("Which of the following is not a symptom of") that pass Tulu's 50% rule on short MMLU items. One DCLM page is the WikiHow article a HellaSwag item was built from, true ending included: real, if minor, contamination for a completion task. run0's own output (2,617 documents) has no 13-gram overlap with any item at all.
rm_units_line: for the 70 flagged web documents, removing whole documents deletes 925,647 characters, the paragraphs containing the match 53,563, the matched span plus 200 characters each side 34,796, and the matched strings alone 6,796 (136 times less than whole documents).
headline: Tulu 3's RLVR prompts contain 70 MMLU high-school-mathematics test questions word for word (26% of that subject), 65 with the MMLU answer as the reward key, yet the set passes Tulu 3's own 2% rule. On the web side, every one of the 43 documents GPT-3's 13-gram rule flags in the samples is a false positive (famous speeches the history items quote, stock phrases). In 1.45 million more FineWeb documents the reading finds 4 pages with a test question among 719 flagged pairs.
canary_line: 1 of 1,867,775 documents across all 12 sets (samples and whole FineWeb files), and 0 of the WARC's 20,991 raw responses (HTML before extraction). The one hit, in the whole FineWeb file, is a forum user's comment page that quotes the BIG-bench canary and another evaluation canary while discussing them: no benchmark data, exactly the caveat in the table. A canary filter would have dropped an innocent page and nothing else here.
pii_note: Presidio with identifier types only finds 80% with 12 false alarms; at score 0.5, 71% with 10.
pii_misses: datatrove (11% recall) is built for two things, emails and public IPv4 addresses, and finds exactly those: it misses the obfuscated emails ("j.morales [at] example [dot] net"), the IPv6 address and everything else, and replaces the role addresses press@ and dpo@ (not personal) and the version number 4.2.1.7. Dolma's regexes (13%) add phones in one US shape and flag private IPs too. The extra regexes (29%) catch cards (with the Luhn check), IBANs, street addresses and handles, nothing else. Presidio (89% with every type) is the only one that finds names, and it pays in false alarms: London, Paris, Jordan and Georgia as places or people, times ("6pm", "Friday") as DATE_TIME, the private IPs. Nobody flags a name with no context ("Text Aisha") reliably, and none treats an age, a job and a town in one sentence (row syn33) as identifying together: the quasi-identifier case.
dolma_url_line: tested here, a sentence with a phone number and a URL keeps its phone span (the URL check returns False); with the pattern as a raw string the check returns True and the phone would be dropped. The post-filter has never worked as written.
pii_real_line: on all 2,617 documents, datatrove's own detector finds 140 emails and 5 public IPs (already replaced, so these are its replacement addresses); Dolma's regexes 119 phone numbers and 8 IPs; the extra regexes 135 phones, 57 street addresses and 47 handles. On a random 500, Presidio (score 0.5 or more, identifiers only) marks 2033 person names, 2197 locations and 3 phone numbers.
wide_line: FineWeb's file 000_00000 of CC-MAIN-2024-30 (971,981 documents, 569 million words) and FineWeb-Edu's (476,676 documents, 395 million words), 0.96 billion words in all.
wide_find: In the two whole FineWeb files, 103 and 212 documents share a 13-gram with some item. Reading all 719 flagged pairs: 582 passages, 127 phrases, 5 WikiHow sources of HellaSwag items, 1 variants and 4 copies: two quiz pages and an article title that ask the same short trivia question as an MMLU item ("How many stars are on the American flag?") without options, and one quiz-aggregator page with an MMLU marketing question and its options. At web scale real copies exist, but they are a few per million documents, and the 13-gram rule finds them only among hundreds of false alarms.
